newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. studies request to bring Pol Pot to justice.
newsitem.headline: U.N. studies request to bring Pol Pot to justice.

text.p: The United Nations is studying how to respond to a request from Cambodia to help bring to justice those responsible for genocide and crimes against humanity during the 1975-79 rule of the Khmer Rouge, a U.N. spokesman said on Monday.

U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said Secretary-General Kofi Annan received a letter from Cambodian Prime Ministers Prince Norodom Sihanouk Ranariddh and Hun Sen following reports that Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot had been captured by former allies.

They wrote that Cambodia "does not have the resources or expertise to conduct this very important procedure. Thus we believe it is necessary to ask for the assistance of the United Nations." They said they were aware of the U.N's response to genocide and crimes against humanity in Rwanda and former Yugoslavia -- a reference to tribunals set up by the U.N. Security Council -- and asked for similar help.

Eckhard said U.N. legal counsel Hans Corell was "looking at what ways, legally, we could accommodate them on this request to bring these people to trial in some kind of an international court." Corell was expected to give the secretary-general a report analysing the options on Monday.

Referring to the crimes attributed to the Khmer Rouge, widely held responsible for the death of more than a million people, the Cambodian prime ministers said: "We are aware that crimes of this magnitude are of concern to all persons in the world, as they greatly diminish respect for the most basic human right, the right to life.

"We hope that the United Nations and international community can assist the Cambodian people in establishing the truth about this period and bringing those responsible to justice. Only in this way can this tragedy be brought to a full and final conclusion."
U.S. officials in Washington said the United States had asked Canada to help extradite Pol Pot from Cambodia so he could be tried by an international tribunal.

At a summit of the eight major industrialised nations in Denver, U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright asked Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy to request the extradition under Canada's law against genocide. Only Canada and Denmark have laws permitting them to make such a request, U.S. officials said.

Canadian officials on Monday said Canada would have a difficult time complying with the request. "It looks like Canada's involvement would be difficult because the legal structure is not in place," Jennifer Ledwidge, a spokeswoman for the Department of Foreign Affairs, said.

Canada has a clause in its criminal code that allows for prosecution for war crimes or crimes against humanity committed outside the country. But it does not have legislation that would enable it to extradite Pol Pot to an international tribunal, Ledwidge said.
